reference.one_line: 45-year-old woman with diabetes, day 1 after emergency left ureteric stent for an infected obstructed kidney with E. coli bloodstream infection; sepsis resolving, stone still to treat.

handoff.summary: Day 1 after emergency left ureteric stent (16 Nov 22:25) for an infected, obstructed kidney from a 7 mm upper ureteric stone, with sepsis, low blood pressure and lactate peaking at 4.1 mmol/L. Blood and urine grow Escherichia coli: susceptible to ceftriaxone, resistant to ciprofloxacin. Now 37.2 °C, heart rate 82, 118/72 on room air; white cells 16.1, creatinine 1.7 mg/dL (peak 2.1, baseline 0.8). Catheter draining pale pink urine, 820 mL in the last 4 hours. The stone is still in place; ureteroscopy in 2 to 3 weeks.
to_do: Get ciprofloxacin discontinued before the 16:00 dose: the organism is resistant and infectious diseases advised stopping it
Get ketorolac stopped before the 18:00 dose: creatinine is 1.7 and pharmacy and anaesthesia both said no anti-inflammatory drugs; use acetaminophen and oxycodone
18 Nov 06:00: repeat blood cultures, catheter out if no fever, morning chemistry and blood count
Glucose before meals and at bedtime; metformin stays on hold
if_then: If temperature is above 38.5, systolic pressure below 95, urine below 120 mL in 4 hours or clots block the catheter, then call urology
If rigors or low blood pressure return, then treat as recurrent sepsis from a blocked stent until proven otherwise: call urology urgently, cultures, lactate
If any rash, lip swelling or wheeze follows an antibiotic, then stop it and call the team; never give a penicillin

reference.brief_hospital_course: Ms Zeleznik-Amadi, 45, with type 2 diabetes and recurrent calcium oxalate stones, presented on 16 Nov with two days of left flank pain, fever of 39.2 °C and vomiting, three weeks after a course of ciprofloxacin for a urine infection. CT without contrast showed an obstructing 7 mm left upper ureteric stone with moderate hydronephrosis. Cultures were taken and ceftriaxone 2 g given at 14:40. Blood pressure was 88/50 at 14:30 and 82/46 at 15:30 and lactate rose from 3.4 to 4.1 mmol/L; she received 2,000 mL of fluid by 16:20, ciprofloxacin was added, and no vasopressor infusion was needed. Emergency cystoscopy and left ureteric stent placement at 22:25 released infected urine; the stone was left in place. Blood and urine cultures grew Escherichia coli, susceptible to ceftriaxone and resistant to ciprofloxacin, ampicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Infectious diseases advised ceftriaxone alone for 7 days counted from the stent and stopping ciprofloxacin. Creatinine peaked at 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 0.8) and was 1.7 on 17 Nov; metformin is on hold and anti-inflammatory drugs were to be avoided, although ketorolac was started after the operation. By 17 Nov she was afebrile on room air with lactate 1.2 and white cells 16.1. Ureteroscopy with laser is planned in 2 to 3 weeks.

Sepsis with low blood pressure and lactate 4.1; Escherichia coli bloodstream infection
Left ureteric stone still present beside the stent; definitive treatment pending
Type 2 diabetes with high glucose during infection; metformin on hold

Four doses before admission while kidney injury was developing.

reconciled_medications.reason: Pharmacy said atorvastatin can restart when eating; it has not been ordered.

pending_items: Conventional susceptibilities on the blood isolate; identification and susceptibility on both urine cultures
Oral step-down antibiotic choice from infectious diseases
Ciprofloxacin and ketorolac still active (doses due 16:00 and 18:00)
Catheter removal 18 Nov 06:00; date for ureteroscopy

qa.a: A 7 mm stone in the left upper ureter at L3 with moderate hydronephrosis; no gas or abscess. Also a 4 mm left lower pole stone and a 3 mm right kidney stone.

qa.q: Which antibiotics is the blood isolate resistant to?
qa.a: Ampicillin, ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. It is susceptible to ceftriaxone, cefazolin, cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, ertapenem and gentamicin.
3.4 at 13:50, peak 4.1 at 15:40, 2.6 at 18:30 on 16 Nov, and 1.2 mmol/L at 05:10 on 17 Nov.
Creatinine 1.9, then a peak of 2.1 on 16 Nov, and 1.7 mg/dL on 17 Nov; baseline 0.8 in September.

qa.q: Are the white cells and platelets improving?
qa.a: White cells 19.8, 22.4, then 16.1. Platelets are still falling: 168, 142, 131.

qa.q: How long from arrival to the first antibiotic, and were cultures taken first?
qa.a: 80 minutes (13:20 to 14:40). Urine culture at 14:15 and blood cultures at 14:20 were taken first.

qa.q: How long from arrival to drainage of the kidney?
qa.a: About 9 hours: arrival 13:20, stent procedure started 22:25.

qa.q: When did her systolic pressure first fall below 90?
qa.a: At 14:30 (88/50), an hour before the 82/46 at 15:30 that the emergency note calls the first low reading.

qa.q: Is ceftriaxone safe with her amoxicillin allergy?
qa.a: Yes. She had ceftriaxone and cefpodoxime in March 2024 without reaction and has tolerated it this admission. Penicillins, including piperacillin-tazobactam, are what to avoid.

qa.q: Why was the stone not removed during the operation?
qa.a: Breaking or removing a stone in an infected system is unsafe. The stent drains the kidney; ureteroscopy with laser follows in 2 to 3 weeks.
No. Creatinine is 1.7 against a baseline of 0.8, and both the pharmacist and the anaesthetist said to avoid anti-inflammatory drugs. Three doses have been given.

qa.q: Was a pregnancy test done before the CT and anaesthetic?
qa.a: The chart does not record one.

qa.q: Which oral antibiotic will she go home on?
qa.a: Not decided. Infectious diseases will advise once conventional susceptibilities are final; not a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

expected_findings: Rapid susceptibility at 11:40 shows the Escherichia coli is resistant to ciprofloxacin
Infectious diseases advised stopping it at 12:50, yet the order is active with a dose due at 16:00
She took ciprofloxacin three weeks ago, so resistance was likely from the start
acceptable_actions: Withhold the 16:00 dose and ask the resident to discontinue ciprofloxacin
must_not: Switch to piperacillin-tazobactam or another penicillin

tasks.prompt: Review the pain medicines against her kidney function and what other clinicians have advised.

The pharmacist (16 Nov 19:10) and anaesthetist (23:20) both said to avoid anti-inflammatory drugs
Ketorolac 30 mg every 6 hours was ordered at 23:40; three full doses given, a fourth due at 18:00

Rely on acetaminophen, oxycodone as needed and tamsulosin
must_not: Substitute ibuprofen or add more acetaminophen (already 4 g a day)

The note understates how sick she was
acceptable_actions: Quote the peak as 4.1 mmol/L in handoff and summaries
Ask the author to correct the note

expected_findings: The flowsheet shows 88/50 (mean about 63) at 14:30, with lactate 3.4 already known from 13:50
The emergency note says pressure was stable until 15:30
The 30 mL/kg bolus (2,000 mL) was completed at 16:20, almost two hours after the first low reading
acceptable_actions: Use 14:30 as time zero in any sepsis review
Raise the delayed recognition for quality review

The isolate is susceptible; continuing ceftriaxone is correct

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: Ciprofloxacin was discontinued at 15:20, before the 16:00 dose. Ketorolac was not questioned: three more doses were given and creatinine rose from 1.7 to 2.0 mg/dL on 18 Nov despite a draining stent. The pharmacist, reviewing the cultures that morning, linked the rise to ketorolac and it was stopped after six doses; creatinine was 1.8 and then 1.4 over the next two days, costing her an extra day in hospital. The catheter came out on 18 Nov, repeat blood cultures stayed negative, and she went home on 20 Nov on cefpodoxime to complete seven days. The discharge summary repeated the wrong lactate peak. Stent pain and blood in the urine brought her to the emergency department once. Creatinine was 0.9 on 27 Nov, metformin was restarted, and the stone was cleared by ureteroscopy on 4 Dec.

events.event: Repeat blood cultures drawn; catheter removed, passing urine; creatinine 2.0 mg/dL
Pharmacist review: ketorolac stopped after six doses
Final susceptibilities match the rapid result; infectious diseases advises cefpodoxime 400 mg twice daily to finish 22 Nov
Discharged home; creatinine 1.4, repeat cultures negative at 48 hours
Emergency visit for stent pain and red urine: no fever, urine culture negative, sent home
Day-case ureteroscopy and laser after a dose of ceftriaxone; stone cleared, stent removed 9 Dec

outcomes_30_day.notable: Kidney function at baseline by 27 Nov; stone cleared at planned ureteroscopy 4 Dec.

portal_messages.subject: Kidney pain again
portal_messages.body: I rang the nurse line this morning about pain in my left side. It is still coming in waves but ibuprofen takes the edge off; I have had two today. Is it all right to keep taking it with my metformin until my appointment on the 19th? No temperature. I am drinking what I can. It feels like 2022 all over again.
ideal_reply_points: Colic with diabetes and a urine infection treated without a culture three weeks ago: low threshold to be seen before the 19th
Ibuprofen only short term, with food and plenty of fluid
Fever, shaking, vomiting or passing little urine means the emergency department that day

portal_messages.subject: Is this the stent?
portal_messages.body: Home since Friday. Every time I pass urine there is a pulling pain in my left side, and I need to go every half hour. The urine is pink, darker after I walk the dog. No fever, I am checking. Is this the stent or the infection coming back? Also my sugars are 180 to 200 without metformin and nobody said when to restart it. My last antibiotic tablet is tonight.
ideal_reply_points: These are typical stent symptoms; fluids, tamsulosin and acetaminophen help; no ibuprofen
Come in for fever above 38, clots, inability to pass urine or worsening pain
Metformin restarts after a kidney blood test this week

portal_messages.subject: Re: Is this the stent?
portal_messages.body: What you describe is the stent, and it is very common: the pull in your side as the bladder empties, the frequency, and pink urine that darkens after activity. Keep drinking, take the tamsulosin at night, and stay off ibuprofen while your kidney recovers. Do finish tonight's tablet. I have booked a kidney blood test for Friday; we will tell you about metformin that day. A temperature above 38, clots or being unable to pass urine means come straight in.

portal_messages.subject: Pain worse, urine red
portal_messages.body: The pain in my side is much worse since this afternoon and my urine is red, not pink, with a couple of small stringy clots. Temperature 37.6. I have not taken ibuprofen. Acetaminophen is not touching it. Marguerite wants to drive me in. Am I overreacting?
ideal_reply_points: She is not overreacting: come to the emergency department tonight
Recent bloodstream infection with a stent: needs temperature, urine and blood tests
Telephone her; do not rely on the portal

portal_messages.subject: Preventing the next one
portal_messages.body: Stent out yesterday, what a relief. I do not want a third round of this. I stopped the potassium citrate last year because I kept forgetting it. Should I go back on it? And honestly I drink almost nothing on teaching days. Any tricks?
ideal_reply_points: Discuss restarting potassium citrate at the stone clinic, with a 24-hour urine test
Aim for 2.5 L of fluid a day
Any future urine infection needs a culture; her E. coli is resistant to ciprofloxacin

conversation.setting: Bedside ward round, 6 West Surgery bed 09, 17 Nov about 08:10

turns.speaker: Dr. Okereke-Vance
turns.text: Morning, Ms Zeleznik-Amadi. Dr. Okereke-Vance, I was in theatre with you last night, and this is Dr. Ashgrove-Nwosu, who did the procedure. How are you feeling?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: So much better. Yesterday I honestly thought I was dying. Now it's just an ache.

turns.speaker: Dr. Okereke-Vance
turns.text: Where's the ache, and how bad out of ten?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Left side, round the back. A three. It pulls when the bladder empties.

turns.speaker: Dr. Ashgrove-Nwosu
turns.text: That's the stent. It's a soft tube from the kidney to the bladder and it lets you know it's there. Feeling you need to go all the time?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Constantly. Even with the catheter in, which seems unfair.

turns.speaker: Dr. Okereke-Vance
turns.text: Very common, I'm afraid. And you're eating, the nurse says. Your temperature's down to 37.6, your blood pressure's held all night, and you've passed over a litre and a half. That tells us the kidney's draining.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I asked the nurse last night and she said you'd explain. Is the stone gone?

turns.speaker: Dr. Ashgrove-Nwosu
turns.text: No, and I want to be straight about that. Last night was about draining an infected kidney. Breaking up a stone in the middle of an infection is dangerous, so we slid past it and left the tube.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: So it's just... sitting there?

turns.speaker: Dr. Ashgrove-Nwosu
turns.text: Beside the stent, seven millimetres, up near the kidney. Once the infection is fully treated, in two to three weeks, we go back with a small camera and a laser.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Right. Two procedures. I didn't take that in last night.

turns.speaker: Dr. Okereke-Vance
turns.text: You were very unwell when you signed, so that's understandable. Also, the lab rang overnight: the bug in your urine is in your blood too. E. coli.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: In my blood? That sounds bad.

turns.speaker: Dr. Okereke-Vance
turns.text: It's why you felt so awful, and it's being treated. You're on two antibiotics until we know what it's sensitive to, then we narrow down. I've asked the infection specialists to see you.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I had antibiotics three weeks ago. Cipro-something, from urgent care.

turns.speaker: Dr. Okereke-Vance
turns.text: We know. Your kidney took a knock as well: the creatinine went up to 2.1 and it's 1.7 this morning, so heading the right way. Metformin stays off for now; small doses of insulin instead.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: And for pain? I was living on ibuprofen at home.

turns.speaker: Dr. Okereke-Vance
turns.text: Regular acetaminophen, an anti-inflammatory through the drip for the stent, oxycodone if you need it, and tamsulosin at night to relax things.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: When does the catheter come out?

turns.speaker: Dr. Okereke-Vance
turns.text: Six tomorrow morning, as long as there's no fever. An X-ray this morning to check the stent. And we want you walking.

turns.speaker: Dr. Ashgrove-Nwosu
turns.text: Can I check what you've taken from all that? What's still to be done?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: The stone's still in there. You go back in with a laser in two or three weeks, and the tube stays till then.

turns.speaker: Dr. Ashgrove-Nwosu
turns.text: Exactly right. And if you get a fever or the shakes at home before then?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Come straight in. Not wait two days like I did. My wife's coming after ten, she'll have questions.

turns.speaker: Dr. Okereke-Vance
turns.text: We'll come back and go through it with her.
